hints: Focus on the two separate ideas here, strength means how much it dissociates, while concentration means how much is dissolved.
A concentrated strong acid puts the maximum possible $\text{H}^+$ into solution, while a dilute weak acid puts in very little $\text{H}^+$.
Remember $\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$, so link the highest $[\text{H}^+]$ to the lowest pH and check which comparison must always hold.
walkthrough:
**Separate strength from concentration**

Strength tells you the proportion dissociated. A strong acid is fully dissociated, a weak acid is only slightly dissociated.

Concentration tells you moles per dm3 dissolved: $$\text{concentration} = \frac{\text{moles}}{\text{volume}}$$

**Link $\text{H}^+$ concentration to pH**

More $\text{H}^+$ means lower pH. This is the key rule:
$$\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$$
So to get the lowest pH, you want high concentration AND strong (full dissociation).

**Apply to option B**

A concentrated strong acid gives a large $[\text{H}^+]$, close to the acid concentration itself.

A dilute weak acid gives a tiny $[\text{H}^+]$, much less than its already low concentration. So the first solution must have lower pH, always.

options.A: Number of H atoms is basicity, not strength. For example, $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ has two H atoms but is weak, while $\text{HCl}$ has one H atom but is strong.
options.B: This is always true. Concentrated plus strong gives maximum $[\text{H}^+]$, dilute plus weak gives minimum $[\text{H}^+]$. Higher $[\text{H}^+]$ always means lower pH.
options.C: This is backwards. A concentrated strong base has very high $[\text{OH}^-]$ and so a very high pH, around 13 to 14. A dilute weak base has low $[\text{OH}^-]$ and a much lower pH, closer to 8 to 9.
options.D: Both a strong acid and a strong base are fully dissociated in dilute aqueous solution. You cannot say one is more dissociated than the other, both are essentially 100% dissociated.
